newsitem.title: USA: GM wins DC press award for safety advances.
newsitem.headline: GM wins DC press award for safety advances.

text.p: General Motors Corp. on Thursday was named the winner of the Washington Automotive Press Association's annual Golden Gear award for contributions to car safety.

The group said that safety clearly was the top car issue of 1996 and "while all sectors of the industry have made great contributions, GM's commitment to safety education and their sheer number of safety innovations stood out."
Past winners have included the designers of the Mazda Motor Corp Miata, car quality surveyor J. D. Power, and Soshiro Honda, founder of Honda Motor Co. Ltd..
The group cited GM safety achievements that included laminated glass windshields, collapsible steering columns. low-cost anti-lock braking systems and crash-test dummies.

Accepting the award, GM's director of safety engineering, Robert Lange, said GM would soon open a major campaign using booklets and videos to promote the proper use of seat belts, child seats and the best way to protect children from the force of deploying airbags.
Asked about the pending new National Highway Traffic Safety Administration airbag regulations, Lange said GM planned to begin installing depowered bags later this year.

The regulations, to go into effect next month, not only call for reducing the inflation power of the bags, but making it easier for car owners to have them disconnected if the owner thinks they pose an unacceptable risk.

While air bags are credited with saving 1,700 lives since introduced in the 1980s, their inflation force of up to 200 miles an hour is blamed for the deaths of at least 32 children and 20 adults, many of them women or frail older people.
Another NHTSA proposal would extend the use of airbag on-off switches for vehicles without rear seats or rear seats that are too small for a child safety seat.
Lange said he thought a better alternative would be for the NHTSA to also allow on-off switches in cars with disconnected airbags so an owner could more easily re-engage the bag for adult passengers.
But, he added, airbags were a net safety gain and if all adults wore seat belts and children were properly restrained in the rear seat, "if we do that, we don't have an airbag problem."
